outcome: No change to the stated conjecture was found; erdosproblems.com's live tracking page for exactly this problem (#28, $500 prize) still lists it as open with no post-2024 developments, and the two candidate 2024 items surfaced by triage are, on inspection, a related-but-different problem (Ding-Zhao) and an unaccepted, uncirculated preprint (Agama) rather than progress on the stated question.
summary: The stated conjecture is Erdős–Turán as it appears verbatim on erdosproblems.com as Problem #28: if A⊆ℕ has A+A containing all but finitely many integers, then limsup 1_A*1_A(n)=∞ (i.e. the representation function of an additive basis of order 2 is unbounded). Thomas Bloom's erdosproblems.com page for this exact problem, last edited December 2025, still lists it as OPEN with a $500 prize, and cites no post-2006 progress on the core statement (the most recent cited advance is Borwein–Choi–Chu 2006, showing f(n) eventually exceeds 7). Two items the triage pass flagged as possibly relevant turned out, on reading, not to bear on this bullet. (1) Ding and Zhao, 'A new upper bound on Ruzsa's numbers on the Erdős-Turán conjecture' (arXiv:2407.02344, v1 2 Jul 2024; published Int. J. Number Theory 20 (2024), 1515-1523) prove limsup_{m→∞} ℓ_m ≤ 144 (improving an earlier bound of 192), where ℓ_m is the minimum average representation-function value over additive bases of the finite cyclic group Z_m — a different, bounded quantity (Ruzsa's number) inspired by the same conjecture but not the statement itself, and not a restriction of it to a sub-case (it's a finite-group analogue with an averaged, not pointwise-limsup, quantity). This is a related problem under §3.1, not a case of the stated conjecture, so it is not counted as a change. (2) Theophilus Agama's arXiv:1707.05679 ('An extension of the Erdős-Turán additive base conjecture via generalized circles of partition') claims in its abstract to prove the conjecture as an application of a 'circle of partition' method, and reached v8 in March 2024 (originally posted 2017, with an intermediate withdrawal in 2017 noted in search results). However: it is classified math.GM (arXiv's General Mathematics catch-all, used for work that hasn't found a home in a refereed subfield listing), it has never been published, and — most tellingly — erdosproblems.com's dedicated, actively maintained page for this exact problem does not mention Agama's claim at all despite listing the problem as open through late 2025. A companion Agama preprint (arXiv:2010.11857) claims variants/generalisations of the conjecture rather than the base statement. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or even a passing mention by specialists tracking this problem was found for either Agama preprint, so neither meets the bar for 'claimed' (which requires the claim to have surfaced as a live claim experts are aware of and are assessing) — it reads as a long-unaccepted preprint the field has not engaged with, not a pending claim, so it does not change the open status. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this space: no lab announcement, paper, or blog credits an AI system with any part of the mathematics for either the stated conjecture or its close variants. The only AI-adjacent artifact found is a Lean formalisation of the problem's *statement* (not a proof) in DeepMind's public 'formal-conjectures' repository (github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, file FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/28.lean), linked from erdosproblems.com — this is a statement formalisation with no proof attached, so per §6.2 it would be formalisation_only/none even if AI-produced, and no source was found describing how that specific Lean file was produced (by a human, an AI, or a mix), so it is noted here but not used to set any field. A web search for an AI system attempting the Erdős-Turán additive basis conjecture surfaced only an unrelated result: OpenAI's LLM improving a bound on the Erdős unit-distance problem (a different, geometric Erdős conjecture), confirmed by reading the Scientific American article directly and finding it concerns points/grids and unit distances, not additive bases.
competing_reading: One could argue the Ding-Zhao bound on ℓ_m (the average representation function over bases of Z_m) is a 'case' of the conjecture restricted to finite cyclic groups rather than a genuinely different problem, in which case it would be `partial` with resolution_direction `null` (a bound moved, not a resolution) — but even under that reading it would be classified `progress`, not `partial`, since nothing was settled either way, only a numeric bound improved on a quantity that remains only conjecturally connected to the infinite-N unboundedness question. I did not adopt this reading because the finite-group average-representation quantity ℓ_m and the integer limsup 1_A*1_A(n) are not the same object connected by a restriction of hypotheses — Ruzsa's number is a separately defined quantity in a separately defined (finite, averaged) setting, motivated by the conjecture but not a sub-case of its statement.
what_would_settle_it: A source (erdosproblems.com update, a survey, or explicit statement in the Ding-Zhao paper's introduction) establishing a formal implication between bounding Ruzsa's number ℓ_m and the original limsup 1_A*1_A(n)=∞ statement would settle whether that work counts as `partial` progress on this exact bullet rather than a related problem; and any statement from a working additive-number-theorist (blog, MathOverflow, or citation) endorsing or refuting Agama's circle-of-partition proof would settle whether that preprint should be elevated to `claimed`.
